vignette:
Rami, a 48-year-old divorced Middle Eastern man who worked as a fashion designer in a busy studio district, had been in his late thirties when the man-made disaster that changed his life unfolded. He had been in a crowded commercial building when the incident began, surrounded by the ordinary materials of his workday—fabric samples, cutting tables, phone calls, the pressure of deadlines—when the event turned abruptly into chaos. In the years since, he has described the memory not as a single story he can tell from beginning to end, but as disconnected pieces that surface without warning: a flash of movement, a section of wall, the sound of people reacting, and one vivid taste that returns with unsettling force when the memory breaks through. He says the event does not feel finished when it comes back to him; instead, it lands in his body as if it is happening again, right then, with no clear boundary between past and present.

At the time, Rami survived, but he came away with the sense that the world could turn dangerous in an instant and that he would not have enough time to understand what was happening before it was already too late. That sense has remained close to the surface. In the months and years afterward, the most ordinary experiences have taken on a sharp, bodily quality because they can pull him back into fragments of that day. He notices nausea first sometimes, a sudden rolling feeling in his stomach that arrives when a memory comes to him without invitation. At other times it is the sensation of a particular temperature on his skin—cool air, an unexpected chill, a shift in the room that seems to match the feeling of that day—and this is enough to make his attention snap backward. When that happens, the memory does not come as a calm recollection. It comes as if the scene is unfolding around him again, immediate and unfinished.

Rami has adapted by building a life around staying ahead of the feeling that danger could return without warning. He checks locks, doors, and windows repeatedly, not because he believes one check is ever enough, but because settling without confirming them leaves him uncomfortable and on edge. Before he can feel at ease in any setting, he identifies escape routes, mentally mapping where he would go if something suddenly went wrong. He does this in restaurants, in office buildings, in showrooms, even in unfamiliar shops while he is sourcing materials for work. His occupation places him in constantly changing environments, and those spaces now require him to perform a silent survey before he can focus on sketches or fittings. He scans for signs of danger wherever he is, his attention tugged away from conversation and design details by exits, hallways, and the movements of other people. He has noticed that this leaves him less able to concentrate, especially when he is trying to work through details that once came easily to him.

To keep himself from being overwhelmed, Rami throws himself into work and other tasks. He stays busy as a way of getting through the day, filling his schedule with errands, revisions, calls, and small obligations so there is less time for his mind to settle on the event. Even so, the pattern has not fully spared him from moments when the memory breaks through. When those moments are strong, he has turned to hurting himself physically to release feelings he experiences as too large to hold inside. He describes these moments not as planned or dramatic, but as desperate attempts to interrupt a surge that feels intolerable.

Over time, the strain of living this way has affected his relationships and his work rhythm. He has found it harder to be fully present with others, especially when he is preoccupied with scanning his surroundings or mentally rehearsing where he would go if something happened. In the studio, he can still do the work, but his concentration is less reliable than it once was, and he often feels he is dividing himself between the task in front of him and the need to stay alert. After years of managing this privately, he finally sought help because the interruptions had become harder to dismiss and harder to contain. What brought him in now was not a single dramatic crisis, but the mounting recognition that the event still arrives in his body as if it is happening again, and that he is increasingly tired of living as though every room might demand an escape. He is most afraid that if he lets himself stop scanning, even briefly, he will be caught unprepared; at the same time, he hopes that treatment might help him feel less trapped by moments that keep pulling him back into a disaster he knows, intellectually, is over, even when it does not feel that way.
